newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians vote in runoff elections.
newsitem.headline: Albanians vote in runoff elections.

text.p: Albanians voted on Sunday in the second round of elections aimed at ending months of anarchy and bloodshed.
The overall contest has already been won by the ex-communist Socialists, who now have a big majority over the right-wing Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha.

The run-off ballots will finalise 34 seats where no one candidate won 50 percent in the first round last Sunday. Counting in seven seats has yet to be completed, the Central Electoral Commission said on Saturday.
The Socialists won about 80 of 155 assembly seats in the first round, ousting Berisha's Democrats after five years in power.
The critical question now is whether the Socialists and their left-wing allies can secure the 20 or so seats needed to get a two-thirds majority in parliament.
That would enable them to make major changes in post-communist laws -- and remove Berisha by parliamentary vote if he fails to honour a pledge to step down if his party were beaten.

Some 150 observers of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe observed the voting under the watchful eye of 7,000 multinational troops dispatched to Albania in April, and soon to be withdrawn.
Tension mounted ahead of the second round as a young man killed when shooting broke out at a monarchist rally this week was buried in a Tirana cemetery.

The defeated Democratic Party, which has blamed the Socialists for his death, urged its supporters to mass at a ceremony in Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square but only a few hundred turned up and the event passed off peacefully.
The head of a Council of Europe parliamentary delegation observing the election on Saturday urged all sides to remain calm.
"This is no time for political bickering and polarisation," Sir Russell Johnston said after meeting key political leaders. "The interests of the country must come first."

The election, Albania's fourth since the 1990 fall of communism, was called in March when the country slid into chaos as angry Albanians took to the street to protest about the failure of popular investment funds. Many blamed the president.

At the height of the rebellion in which 1,500 people have died, Berisha agreed to hold a new election, replacing a May 1996 poll that was boycotted by the Socialists and described by international observers as seriously flawed.
A multi-party government headed by a Socialist was appointed in the interim.

Based on preliminary results early last week which the OSCE described as "adequate and acceptable", Berisha has already conceded defeat and promised to honour a campaign pledge to step down once a new leftist government is installed.

But in recent days Berisha's Democrats appear to have joined forces with Albania's self-proclaimed King Leka I who has denounced the results of a referendum, held alongside last Sunday's vote, which rejected reinstatement of the monarchy.

Several Berisha stalwarts were defeated in the first round while others face tough run-off battles. With the south, focal point of the rebellion, voting solidly against the president, most contests are in the north of the mountainous country.

Former Democratic prime minister Aleksander Meksi, ousted in March when the multi-party government was appointed, faces a Socialist in Tirana and Fatos Beja, a top Berisha adviser, is contesting another seat in the capital.

In Kavaje, southwest of Tirana, two veteran Democrats face second-round battles. Party leader Tritan Shehu takes on a member of the anti-Berisha Rightist Union while former Interior Minister Halit Shamata is up against a Socialist.
